paragraphs.heading: A period between two eras
paragraphs.text: The early modern period covers roughly 1500 to 1800. Its divisions come mainly from the history of Europe and from the wider idea of modernity. In Europe it is the time after the Middle Ages and before the arrival of modernity, but no single date marks its start or end, and scholars do not agree on where the boundaries fall.

paragraphs.heading: Where it starts and stops
paragraphs.text: Historians have put forward several starting points: the Renaissance, the printing revolution that began in the 1440s, the Age of Discovery, the start of the Reformation, or the year 1453, when Constantinople fell. Those who stress globalization also point to the Columbian contact, which brought the notion of a New World joining the Old. The period gave way to the late modern era in the late 18th century, with the Industrial Revolution, the American and French Revolutions and Napoleon's rise to power.

paragraphs.heading: A name for an age
paragraphs.text: The historian of the Middle Ages Lynn Thorndike was the first to propose early modern as the name of a distinct period of European history. In his 1926 book A Short History of Civilization, he offered it as a broader alternative to the Renaissance. Economic historians took it up in the 1940s and 1950s, and by the 1990s it was widely known among scholars, more so in North America than in Europe. From the 1980s some scholars applied it outside Europe, for example to Tokugawa Japan.

paragraphs.heading: A world drawn together
paragraphs.text: In recent decades, historians have argued that, seen from a worldwide view, the period's key feature was the spread of globalization. Parts of the globe that had been isolated came into lasting contact, above all through the Columbian Exchange between the Old World and the New, which greatly changed the human environment. Europeans began colonizing the Americas and set up trading hubs in Asia and Africa, and the Atlantic slave trade began. New economies and institutions grew more sophisticated and more globally linked, and mercantilism rose to become the dominant economic theory.

paragraphs.heading: Upheaval in Europe
paragraphs.text: In Europe, feudalism declined, the Crusades ended, and so did Western Europe's religious unity under the Roman Catholic Church. The Protestant Reformation shook the old order, triggering a backlash that widened the Inquisition and set off the wars of religion, among them the bloody Thirty Years' War. Those wars closed with the Peace of Westphalia, which set up the modern international system. The age also brought the Scientific Revolution, quickening technical progress, and better maps and ship designs that made travel faster.

paragraphs.heading: The Gunpowder Empires
paragraphs.text: Beyond Europe, the Ottomans took Southeastern Europe along with parts of North Africa and West Asia. The Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires, traditionally called the Gunpowder Empires, consolidated power across the Islamic world. Firearms and artillery were decisive in their expansion, but their strength also rested on centralized states, efficient bureaucracies, tax collection and control of key trade routes. The Mughal Empire is thought to have had the largest economy in the world, worth 25% of global GDP.
